name: SeekStorm
workload: BM25 lexical search on English Wikipedia (5,032,105 docs, 8.28GB decompressed) using AOL-query-derived intersection/union/frequent-term/phrase queries, single-threaded, via the open-source 'search-benchmark-game' harness (forked from Tantivy/Jason Wolfe's benchmark)
claimed_speedup: vs Lucene: 4.6x-10.1x on typical single/multi-field 'all', 'union' and 'intersection' queries; up to 174.8x-734.1x on pathological single-very-frequent-term ('the') and two-phase-critic queries (vs Tantivy: 1x-6.1x typical, up to ~835x on the same frequent-term queries)
hardware: ThinkPad P1, 64.0 GB RAM, Intel Core i7-13700H 2.40GHz, 2TB Hynix NVMe SSD (per the Dec 2023 blog post). A later re-run of the same open-source search-benchmark-game harness, documented in github.com/SeekStorm/search-benchmark-game (README), used the same ThinkPad P1 Gen 6 / i7-13700H under Ubuntu 24.04 with Rust 1.90 and OpenJDK 21, but that run's raw results (results.json, versions tantivy-0.25/lucene-10.3.0-bp/seekstorm-1.0.0) were not re-aggregated into summary multipliers by us.
tradeoffs: Rust, single binary, no JVM/segment-merge GC pauses (claimed benefit for tail latency); newer project than Lucene/Tantivy with a smaller ecosystem and fewer production deployments; benchmark adapters are written by each engine's own authors ('for maximum authenticity') rather than a fully neutral third party.
caveats: Headline numbers are from a Dec 2023 first-party blog post using older engine versions, not the current results.json in the SeekStorm/search-benchmark-game repo. The extreme 100-800x multipliers occur only on a single very-frequent term ('the') and a two-term phrase+filter query, and plausibly reflect algorithmic handling of very common terms (block-max pruning) rather than a general throughput advantage; typical multi-term intersection/union queries show a much more modest 1.6x-10.1x edge over Lucene. Exact compiler flags for the JVM (Lucene) and rustc (SeekStorm) build are not stated on the cited page, so tier is capped at B rather than A.
found_via: Hacker News: 'faster than Lucene' -> Show HN: Search-as-a-service: 20x faster than Lucene and 30x more queries/dollar (HN 25210776); Show HN: SeekStorm open-source sub-millisecond search in Rust (HN 42295792)

name: ugrep (with ugrep-indexer)
workload: Cold-filesystem recursive search for the pattern 'std::chrono' across the ugrep v3.12.6 source tree (1,317 files, 28 directories, 12.2MB), with OS file-system cache cleared by unmounting/remounting the drive; 8 threads
claimed_speedup: README states ugrep's own indexed cold search (0.0487s best-of-4, range 0.0487-0.0983s) is '21 times faster' (10x-21x across runs) than ugrep's own unindexed cold search (1.02s); ripgrep 13.0.0 took 1.18s on the same cold search, i.e. roughly 12x-24x faster than ripgrep for the indexed run (derived from page data). Without indexing, plain ugrep (1.02s) was already marginally faster than ripgrep (1.18s) on this query.
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (ugrep); ugrep-indexer companion tool is a separate, smaller repo (84 stars)
tradeoffs: Speed advantage requires running the separate ugrep-indexer tool ahead of time to build per-directory N-gram Bloom-filter index files (~4KB/file storage overhead at default accuracy, tunable 0-9); index has a false-positive rate so some non-matching files are still opened; benefit is specific to cold/uncached file systems -- on a warm page cache, indexed search adds overhead and may not be faster; index must be kept up to date (incremental re-indexing) as files change.
caveats: Numbers come from the project's own README with exact commands shown, but no CPU model, OS, or compiler flags are stated, and the dataset is small (1,317 files); this caps the tier at C rather than A/B. The '21x' figure as stated compares indexed vs. ugrep's own unindexed run, not directly vs. ripgrep -- the ~12x-24x vs-ripgrep figure is derived by us from the same page's numbers.
found_via: Hacker News: 'ugrep' -> Show HN 'Ugrep-indexer: A monotonic indexer to speed up grepping by >10x' (HN 37097176); 'Ugrep - a more powerful, fast, user-friendly, compatible grep' (HN 38819262)

name: Manticore Search
workload: Independent db-benchmarks.com suite: full-text/analytics queries over a 1.7-billion-row taxi dataset (32-core SSD server), 1.1M curated Hacker News comments, and 10M nginx log lines; plus bulk-load of 1.7B docs via Logstash vs Manticore's built-in indexer, and direct-load throughput of 50M random documents
claimed_speedup: 4x faster queries than 'tuned Elasticsearch' on the 1.7B-doc taxi dataset; 15x faster on the 1.1M Hacker-News-comments test; 22x faster on the 10M-row nginx-log analytics test; ~25x faster bulk ingestion of 1.7B docs (1h08m vs 28h33m via Logstash, 32 shards); ~5.5x higher indexing throughput (894,856 vs 162,614 docs/sec) loading 50M random documents
hardware: 32-core server with SSD (stated only for the 1.7B-document taxi-dataset test; CPU model and hardware are not restated for the other three sub-tests)
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 copyleft (vs Elasticsearch's SSPL/Elastic license) may restrict some proprietary embedding; SQL-like + JSON query interface differs from Elasticsearch's Query DSL; smaller ecosystem/plugin base than the Elastic stack; historically forked from the Sphinx search engine.
caveats: The benchmark numbers are republished on Manticore's own blog, though they cite the independent, open-source db-benchmarks.com suite (github.com/db-benchmarks/db-benchmarks) rather than a Manticore-only test. CPU/RAM details are given for only one of the four cited sub-tests, and neither compiler flags nor exact Elasticsearch/Manticore versions are stated on the cited page, so tier is capped at B. Elasticsearch itself is Lucene-based, so this is an indirect comparison to the Lucene baseline rather than a direct Lucene-library benchmark.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Manticore Search' -> 'Manticore Search: Fast, efficient, drop-in replacement for Elasticsearch' (HN 44658978); 'An objective comparison between Elasticsearch and Manticore Search' (HN 32483864)
